public_rationale: The narrow possibility claim is supported. The controlled rule-discovery experiment shows that feedback functioning as an echo chamber can leave users less likely to discover an accurate hypothesis than independent feedback. This is an ordinary instance of being kept from finding a better idea. Support is qualified: one planned discovery comparison was not significant, and evidence from other decision tasks shows that sycophantic advice can still be informative overall. Neither limitation overturns the claim that impairment can occur.
limitations: Support concerns accurate hypothesis discovery in a short experimental task.
The experiment does not establish that all chatbots, users, or forms of brainstorming are harmed.
Feedback selection supplies the demonstrated mechanism; the study does not isolate every feature commonly called sycophancy.

criteria.support_condition: A controlled human study demonstrates that confirmation-biased AI feedback can reduce discovery of accurate or better hypotheses compared with informative or independently selected feedback.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Strong direct evidence refutes the proposed discovery-impairing mechanism under the relevant echo-chamber conditions. One null result or beneficial outcomes in other tasks would not alone refute a possibility claim.

evidence.publisher: arXiv; Rafael M. Batista and Thomas L. Griffiths
evidence.explanation: Default feedback resembled explicitly confirming feedback; discovery was 5.9% with default feedback versus 29.5% with independent samples, an exploratory difference with p<.001. However, the confirming-versus-disconfirming comparison was not significant (p=.143), limiting the strength of that particular contrast.

The prospective protocol specifies randomized feedback conditions and an objective rule-discovery outcome. No data had been collected at registration; the completed paper was public in February, establishing 2026 as the experiment year.
